title: Subsequences and Bolzano-Weierstrass
objectives: Prove that every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

screens.title: Two limits, no limit
screens.prose: A **subsequence** $(a_{n_k})$ picks indices $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$. Here $(a_{2k}) = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2k} \to 1$ and $(a_{2k-1}) \to -1$.
screens.question: What does this say about $(a_n)$ itself?

options.text: It diverges: if $a_n \to L$, every subsequence would tend to $L$, but these tend to 1 and $-1$.
It converges to 0, the average of 1 and $-1$.
options.why: You averaged the two strands. No term is near 0: every $|a_n| > 1$.

options.text: It converges to 1, the limit of the upper strand.
options.why: You kept one strand. The odd terms stay near $-1$, outside any thin band round 1.
You allowed two limits. A limit is unique; two different subsequential limits mean there is none.

hints.text: If the whole sequence had a limit $L$, what would each strand tend to?
Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.
The strands tend to 1 and $-1$, which differ. So no $L$ exists.

feedback.correct: Right. Two different subsequential limits prove divergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a limit of the whole sequence would force on each strand.

byKey.zero: You averaged 1 and $-1$. Every term has $|a_n| > 1$, so none is within 1 of 0.

explain.text: If $a_n \to L$, both strands would tend to $L$, so $L = 1$ and $L = -1$ at once. That is impossible. So $(a_n)$ diverges; next we prove the fact this used.

screens.title: What counts as a subsequence
screens.prose: A subsequence keeps the order of the original and never reuses an index: $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$, strictly.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which lists are subsequences?

options.why: You allowed a repeated index. Each term of the original may be used once; $n_1 < n_2$ is strict.
You allowed the indices to go back. A subsequence keeps the original order, so the indices must rise.

hints.text: Check whether each list of indices strictly increases.
B repeats 1; C goes from 3 back to 1.
Only A and D strictly increase.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A subsequence needs strictly increasing indices.

byKey.B: You counted B. Its indices repeat, so it is not a subsequence, even though each value appears in $(a_n)$.

explain.text: A and D rise strictly, so they are subsequences. B repeats indices, and C goes backwards. With $a_n = (-1)^n(1 + \tfrac1n)$, list B would read $-2, -2, 1.5, 1.5, \dots$, which uses terms twice.

screens.title: Why $n_k \ge k$
screens.prose: The proof that subsequences keep the limit needs one small fact: $n_k \ge k$ for every $k$. For list D, $n_k = k^2 \ge k$.
screens.question: Why is $n_k \ge k$ for any subsequence?

options.text: By induction: $n_1 \ge 1$, and $n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k$ gives $n_{k+1} \ge k + 1$, since indices are whole numbers.

options.why: You used one example. List D has $n_k = k^2$; the fact must hold for every subsequence.
You took the whole sequence as the only case. In list A, $n_3 = 6 \ne 3$.
You used growth without a rate. $n_k \to \infty$ alone does not give $n_k \ge k$ at each $k$; the strict rise does.

hints.text: Start at $k = 1$: what is the least $n_1$ can be?
Each step $n_{k+1} > n_k$ raises the index by at least 1.
So $n_{k+1} \ge n_k + 1 \ge k + 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. Strictly rising whole numbers gain at least 1 per step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use that the indices are whole numbers and rise strictly.

explain.text: $n_1 \ge 1$ because indices start at 1. If $n_k \ge k$, then $n_{k+1} \ge n_k + 1 \ge k + 1$. So the $k$th index is never behind $k$.

screens.title: Subsequences keep the limit
screens.prose: Prove: if $a_n \to L$, then every subsequence $a_{n_k} \to L$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $(a_{n_k})$ be a subsequence and let $\varepsilon > 0$.
Since $a_n \to L$, choose $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
So $|a_{n_k} - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge N$, and $a_{n_k} \to L$. $\blacksquare$
Choose $N$ with $|a_{n_k} - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge N$.
lines.why: You assumed what we are proving. The $N$ must come from the convergence of $(a_n)$.
You took the indices to be $1, 2, 3, \dots$ In general only $n_k \ge k$ holds.

hints.text: Get $N$ from the whole sequence first.
Then use $n_k \ge k$ to land $n_k$ past $N$.
Order: set up, $N$ from $a_n \to L$, $n_k \ge k \ge N$, conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. The same $N$ works for the subsequence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The definition for $(a_n)$ supplies $N$; then $n_k \ge k$ does the rest.

byKey.d1: You chose $N$ for the subsequence directly. That is the conclusion; it must be derived.
byKey.d2: You set $n_k = k$. For list A, $n_k = 2k$; the proof needs only $n_k \ge k$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The $N$ for $(a_n)$ works for the subsequence too. If $k \ge N$, then $n_k \ge k \ge N$, so $a_{n_k}$ lies in the band. So subsequences of a convergent sequence share its limit.

screens.title: Ten halvings
screens.prose: Keep halving $[-2, 2]$. The kept intervals are nested, and each is half the one before.
screens.question: How long is the interval after 10 halvings?

hints.text: The start has length 4.
Each halving divides the length by 2.
After 10 halvings: $\tfrac{4}{2^{10}} = \tfrac{4}{1024}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from length 4 and halve it 10 times.

byKey.nine: You halved 9 times. Ten halvings give $\tfrac{4}{1024}$, not $\tfrac{4}{512}$.
byKey.unit: You started from length 1. $[-2, 2]$ has length 4, so the answer is 4 times $\tfrac{1}{1024}$.
byKey.tenth: You divided by 10 once. Each halving divides by 2, ten times over.

explain.text: Length $\tfrac{4}{2^k}$ after $k$ halvings, so $\tfrac{4}{1024} \approx 0.0039$ after 10. The lengths tend to 0. By completeness, nested closed intervals like these share exactly one point.

screens.title: Why a good half exists
screens.prose: The proof needs, at every step, a half holding $a_n$ for infinitely many $n$. Suppose the current interval $I_k$ holds infinitely many.
screens.question: Why must one of its halves hold infinitely many too?

options.text: If each half held finitely many, $I_k$ would hold finitely many in all, which is false.
Because the terms are spread evenly over the interval.
options.why: You assumed an even spread. The terms can crowd one half, as ours crowd $(1, 1.5]$.

options.text: Because the left half always does.
options.why: You fixed a side. In our example $[0, 1]$, the left half, held none.
You assumed convergence. Bolzano-Weierstrass is for sequences such as $(-1)^n$ that may not converge.

hints.text: Count: the terms in $I_k$ are the terms in its two halves together.
Two finite counts add to a finite count.
So if $I_k$ holds infinitely many, both halves cannot hold finitely many.

feedback.correct: Right. Finite plus finite is finite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens if both halves held finitely many terms.

explain.text: Every term in $I_k$ lies in one half or the other. Two finite sets have a finite union. So if $I_k$ holds infinitely many terms, at least one half does too.

screens.title: Bolzano-Weierstrass proved
screens.prose: Prove: every bounded sequence, $|a_n| \le M$, has a convergent subsequence. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $I_1 = [-M, M]$, which holds every term, and pick $n_1 = 1$.
Halve $I_k$. One half holds $a_n$ for infinitely many $n$; call it $I_{k+1}$.
Pick $n_{k+1} > n_k$ with $a_{n_{k+1}} \in I_{k+1}$, possible since infinitely many indices qualify.
The $I_k$ are nested, with lengths $\tfrac{2M}{2^{k-1}} \to 0$. By completeness they share a point $x$.
Both $a_{n_k}$ and $x$ lie in $I_k$, so $|a_{n_k} - x| \le \tfrac{2M}{2^{k-1}} \to 0$. $\blacksquare$
Pick $n_{k+1}$ with $a_{n_{k+1}} \in I_{k+1}$, perhaps equal to $n_k$.
lines.why: You allowed a repeated index. A subsequence needs $n_{k+1} > n_k$, which infinitely many choices make possible.

lines.text: The intervals shrink to $x$, so $a_n \to x$.
lines.why: You concluded about the whole sequence. Only the chosen terms lie in every $I_k$; $(-1)^n$ shows the rest may wander.

hints.text: Start with the interval that holds everything, then describe one step of halving.
After the halving and the choice of index, the nested intervals give the point $x$.
Order: start, halve, pick a later index, nested intervals, conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. Halve, keep, pick a later index, and let completeness give the point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step halves, keeps a good half, and picks a strictly later index.

byKey.d1: You let $n_{k+1} = n_k$. That repeats a term, so the result is not a subsequence.
byKey.d2: You claimed $a_n \to x$. The proof controls only the subsequence; $(-1)^n$ is bounded and diverges.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The halving keeps infinitely many terms in each $I_k$, so a later index is always available. The nested intervals shrink to one point $x$ by completeness. The chosen terms are trapped with $x$, so $a_{n_k} \to x$.

options.text: No. It promises a convergent subsequence. $a_n = (-1)^n(1 + \tfrac1n)$ is bounded, its even terms converge, and it diverges.

options.text: Yes, but only for monotone sequences.
options.why: You merged two theorems. Monotone convergence needs monotone; Bolzano-Weierstrass needs only bounded and gives less.

options.text: No. The theorem is about unbounded sequences.
options.why: You reversed the hypothesis. The theorem needs a bounded sequence.

hints.text: Look at the sequence on the screen: is it bounded, and does it converge?

screens.title: Estimates that will not settle

options.why: You read the theorem as convergence. It promises only a convergent subsequence, and here there are two different ones.

options.text: No subsequence can converge, because the estimates jump.

hints.text: Bounded: what does Bolzano-Weierstrass promise?

feedback.correct: Right. Two cluster points point to two regimes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the theorem promises, and how many subsequential limits you see.

explain.text: Bolzano-Weierstrass guarantees a cluster point for any bounded sequence of estimates. Here there are two, near 0.18 and 0.41. Two subsequential limits mean the estimates diverge: model the regimes rather than wait for convergence.

ideas: A subsequence $(a_{n_k})$ uses indices $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$, so $n_k \ge k$. If $a_n \to L$, every subsequence tends to $L$.
Two subsequences with different limits prove divergence: in $(-1)^n(1 + \tfrac1n)$ the evens tend to 1 and the odds to $-1$.
Bolzano-Weierstrass: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. Halve, keep a half with infinitely many terms, and pick a later index.

formula.name: Bolzano-Weierstrass
formula.tex: |a_n| \le M\ \forall n \;\Rightarrow\; \exists\, n_1 < n_2 < \cdots:\ a_{n_k} \to x
formula.note: After $k$ halvings of $[-M, M]$ the interval has length $\tfrac{2M}{2^k}$.
